title: Class 5 Maths Time Chapter: 24-Hour Clock, Timetables & Elapsed Time + Free Quiz
meta_title: Class 5 Maths Time: Clocks & Timetables + Quiz
meta_desc: Master the Class 5 maths time chapter: 24-hour clock, elapsed time, and reading train timetables through solved case studies, plus a free 8-question quiz.
excerpt: Time is the one Class 5 topic that shows up on every family train journey. Here is how to teach the 24-hour clock, elapsed time and timetable reading through two solved case studies, with a quick quiz to test what stuck.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Stand on any platform at Nagpur Junction and you will hear a parent squint at the board and mutter, ‘22:15… so that is quarter past ten at night?’ That small hesitation is exactly what the class 5 maths time chapter is meant to fix. By Grade 5 a child is no longer just reading a clock face — they are converting between the 12-hour and 24-hour systems, working out how long a journey takes, and pulling the right row out of a train timetable. These are not textbook tricks. They are the sums a ten-year-old will actually use on the next family trip.

In my experience, the topic goes wrong when it is taught as isolated conversions on a worksheet. Children can turn 14:30 into 2:30 p.m. all day and still freeze when a real timetable asks them a question. So I teach it the other way round: start with a journey, then let the clock skills fall out of it. Below are the three ideas that matter, followed by two worked case studies of the kind you will find in the practice book.

The 24-hour clock: the part most children rush

The rule is simple and worth drilling until it is automatic. From midnight to noon the two systems agree, except that you write two digits: 6 a.m. is 06:00. After noon you add 12 to the hour: 1 p.m. becomes 13:00, 5 p.m. becomes 17:00, 11 p.m. becomes 23:00. Midnight is 00:00 and noon is 12:00 — the two that trip up even adults.

Here is the conversion table I stick on the fridge for a fortnight.

12-hour time24-hour timeEveryday moment
6:00 a.m.06:00School bus leaves
12:00 noon12:00Lunch break
3:45 p.m.15:45Tuition starts
8:30 p.m.20:30Dinner
12:00 midnight00:00Day changes

Elapsed time: count up, do not subtract blindly

Ask a child how long it is from 09:40 to 11:25 and many will try to subtract the whole thing in one go, borrowing wrongly because minutes are in sixties, not tens. The reliable method is to count up in friendly jumps. From 09:40, jump 20 minutes to 10:00, then 1 hour to 11:00, then 25 minutes to 11:25. Add the pieces: 20 + 60 + 25 = 105 minutes, which is 1 hour 45 minutes.

Why the jump method beats column subtraction

Column subtraction of time fails quietly. A child writes 11:25 − 09:40, sees that 25 is smaller than 40, and either gets a negative or invents a rule. Counting up never produces a negative, and it mirrors how we actually think about waiting time. I only introduce formal subtraction once the jumps are second nature.

Reading a timetable without getting lost

A timetable is just a table where each column is a station and each row is a train. The two skills are (a) find the cell where your train meets your station, and (b) subtract two cells to get a duration. The mistake to warn children about: reading across the wrong row. Teach them to place a finger or ruler under the row before reading.

  • Find your boarding station column, then your train’s row — that cell is departure.
  • Find your destination station column in the same row — that cell is arrival.
  • Elapsed time from departure to arrival is the journey length.
  • Watch for times that cross midnight — the arrival day may be the next date.

Case study 1: the morning train to Pune

Read the passage, then work each question. This is the exact format of the solved case studies in the practice book.

The Deccan Express leaves Mumbai at 06:15 and reaches Pune at 09:40. Aarav’s family reaches the station at 05:50. The train halts at Lonavala at 08:05 for 4 minutes.

  • How long before departure did they reach? From 05:50 to 06:15 is 25 minutes.
  • How long is the whole journey? Count up from 06:15: 45 minutes to 07:00, then 2 hours to 09:00, then 40 minutes to 09:40. That is 45 + 120 + 40 = 205 minutes, or 3 hours 25 minutes.
  • What time does the train leave Lonavala? 08:05 plus a 4-minute halt is 08:09.

Case study 2: planning a birthday afternoon

Meera’s party starts at 16:30. The cake is ordered for 15:45, games run for 90 minutes from the start, and guests leave 30 minutes after the games end.

  • Write 16:30 in 12-hour time. 16 − 12 = 4, so it is 4:30 p.m.
  • When do the games finish? 16:30 plus 90 minutes is 18:00, that is 6:00 p.m.
  • When do guests leave? 18:00 plus 30 minutes is 18:30, or 6:30 p.m.
  • How long before the party does the cake arrive? From 15:45 to 16:30 is 45 minutes.

Notice how each answer used one of the three core skills. That is the point of case studies — they force a child to choose the right tool instead of being told which conversion to do.

A one-week plan that works

Ten minutes a day beats a marathon on Sunday. Two days on 24-hour conversions, two days on elapsed-time jumps, one day on a real timetable printed from any railway site, and the weekend on mixed case studies. One honest caveat: do not push speed early. A child who reasons out 205 minutes slowly is in far better shape than one who guesses fast.

Try the quiz, then the case studies

The free 8-question quiz below covers everything here — 24-hour conversions, elapsed time and a timetable read. Let your child attempt it and read the explanations together for anything they miss. quiz.title: Class 5 Maths Time Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on the 24-hour clock, elapsed time and reading a timetable. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Class 5 time: 24-hour clock, duration and timetables

questions.explanation: After noon, subtract 12 from the hour: 17 − 12 = 5, and it is afternoon, so 5:00 p.m.

questions.q: How do you write 9:20 p.m. on a 24-hour clock?
questions.explanation: Add 12 to the p.m. hour: 9 + 12 = 21, so it is 21:20.

questions.q: How long is it from 08:30 to 10:15?
questions.explanation: Count up: 30 minutes to 09:00, then 1 hour to 10:00, then 15 minutes. 30 + 60 + 15 = 105 minutes = 1 hour 45 minutes.

questions.q: A train leaves at 14:10 and arrives at 16:40. How long is the journey?
questions.explanation: From 14:10 to 16:10 is 2 hours, then 30 more minutes to 16:40. Total 2 hours 30 minutes.

questions.q: What time is midnight on a 24-hour clock?
questions.explanation: Midnight is written 00:00, the moment the date changes. Noon is 12:00.

questions.q: A bus at 07:55 is delayed by 20 minutes. What is the new departure time?
questions.explanation: 07:55 plus 20 minutes: 5 minutes reaches 08:00, then 15 more makes 08:15.

questions.q: How many minutes are there in 2 hours 25 minutes?
questions.explanation: 2 hours is 120 minutes, plus 25 minutes gives 145 minutes.

questions.q: A film starts at 18:45 and lasts 2 hours 30 minutes. When does it end?
questions.explanation: 18:45 plus 2 hours is 20:45, plus 30 more minutes is 21:15, that is 9:15 p.m.

faq.q: What does the Class 5 maths time chapter cover?
faq.a: It covers reading and writing the 24-hour clock, converting between 12-hour and 24-hour time, calculating elapsed time or duration, and reading calendars and railway or bus timetables to plan real journeys.

faq.q: What is the easiest way to teach elapsed time?
faq.a: Count up in friendly jumps instead of subtracting in one go. From 09:40 to 11:25, jump 20 minutes to 10:00, 1 hour to 11:00, then 25 minutes — add the pieces to get 1 hour 45 minutes. It never produces a wrong negative.

faq.q: How do you convert p.m. times to the 24-hour clock?
faq.a: For any time after noon, add 12 to the hour: 1 p.m. is 13:00, 6 p.m. is 18:00, 11 p.m. is 23:00. Morning times keep the same hour with two digits, so 7 a.m. is 07:00. Midnight is 00:00.

faq.q: Why use case studies to teach time?
faq.a: A conversion drill tells a child which operation to do. A case study — a train passage or a party plan — makes them choose the right skill themselves, which is where real understanding shows up in exams and in life.
